summary: Describes updated methods for handling Unicode usernames and passwords. It replaces SASLprep and stringprep with the more maintainable PRECIS approach. It was replaced by RFC 8265.

eli5.summary: Rules so fancy characters in names and passwords are treated the same everywhere.

subtitle: How to clean up, normalize and compare Unicode usernames and passwords so that look-alike characters do not cause false matches.

tldr.problem: Usernames and passwords can contain any Unicode character, and a naive comparison lets look-alike characters match (or fail to match) in ways that confuse users and open the door to spoofing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three profiles of the PRECIS framework: two for usernames (case mapped or case preserved) and one for passwords (OpaqueString). Each fixes the rules for width mapping, case, normalization and direction, and strings are compared octet for octet after those rules are applied.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the older SASLprep profile (RFC 4013). It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8265.

today: RFC 7613 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8265, which is the version to follow now. It in turn replaced the SASLprep approach of RFC 4013.

sections.title: Why Usernames and Passwords Need Rules
sections.content:
Usernames and passwords are sent as plain text (as in the SASL PLAIN mechanism and HTTP Basic) or fed into a cryptographic function such as a hash (as in SCRAM and HTTP Digest). Either way, two strings that look the same to a person must be treated as the same by software, and strings that are really different must not be confused.

The RFC gives an example of the danger: it would be dangerous to treat SUPERSCRIPT ONE (U+00B9) as equal to DIGIT ONE (U+0031), because an attacker could then spoof an account such as user1@example.com. The rules here are written as profiles of the PRECIS framework from RFC 7564.

The RFC does not change existing protocols by itself. A protocol that uses the old SASLprep rules keeps them until its own community explicitly updates it, because uncoordinated changes can hurt interoperability and security. The methods are also not meant for strings that are not usernames (such as LDAP distinguished names) or for secrets that are not strings, such as keys and certificates.
sections.eli5: Imagine two kids who both write their name but one uses fancy handwriting. We want the teacher to see they are the same name, but not to mix up two kids who only look alike.

sections.title: Usernames: Userparts and Two Profiles
sections.content:
A username is a string of Unicode code points encoded as UTF-8 and made of one or more userparts separated by spaces. Each userpart may contain only code points allowed by the PRECIS IdentifierClass, which means almost only letters and digits. Constructions like user@example.com are allowed. A username MUST NOT be zero bytes long, and that check happens after normalization and mapping.

Two profiles exist, and they differ only in the case-mapping rule:

  • UsernameCaseMapped maps uppercase and titlecase characters to lowercase, preferably using Unicode Default Case Folding.
  • UsernameCasePreserved does not map case.

Both profiles apply the same ordered rules: map fullwidth and halfwidth characters to their decomposition mappings, no additional mapping, the case rule above, Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC), and the Bidi Rule from RFC 5893 for strings with right-to-left characters. Two strings are equal only if they match octet for octet after this processing.

The RFC suggests the case-mapped profile is generally preferable, because not mapping case can cause false positives in authentication and confuse users. The case-preserved profile can still make sense for backward compatibility with deployed systems. Protocols MUST say whether and when case mapping applies, and SHOULD delay it to the last possible moment, such as when looking up or comparing a username.
sections.eli5: For names, you can choose to treat BIG and small letters as the same, or to keep them different. The rulebook says picking "same" is usually safer, but either is allowed if you say which one you picked.

sections.title: Username Examples
sections.content:
The RFC lists userparts that are legal and strings that are not. Legal ones include juliet@example.com, fussball, the German spelling with the sharp s (U+00DF), and Greek letters such as small pi (U+03C0).

Several subtle points follow. The sharp s and "ss" spellings are different userparts, so a server wanting to avoid confusion would need a registration policy that blocks one if the other exists. Greek capital sigma (U+03A3) and small sigma (U+03C3) match if case is mapped, but final sigma (U+03C2) does not match either, because the PRECIS rules do not account for it.

Not valid as userparts: one containing a space (though that is still a valid username, being two userparts), an empty string, a string with ROMAN NUMERAL FOUR (U+2163), which has a compatibility equivalent, and one with BLACK CHESS KING (U+265A), because symbols are not in the IdentifierClass.

Spaces can also be used at the application layer to build things like "Firstname Middlename Lastname" out of several userparts.
sections.eli5: Some letters look alike but are different, like a double-s and a special German letter. The rules say they stay different unless the website chooses to block one of them.

sections.title: Passwords: The OpaqueString Profile
sections.content:
A password is a UTF-8 string that conforms to the OpaqueString profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass. Because the goal is to allow as many characters as possible (more entropy), the rules are looser than for usernames. A password MUST NOT be zero bytes long after normalization and mapping. The RFC notes this is not a strength rule, since one byte is highly insecure; it prevents software from accidentally omitting the password altogether.

Enforcement applies these rules in order:

  • Fullwidth and halfwidth characters are NOT mapped.
  • Any non-ASCII space (Unicode category Zs other than U+0020) is mapped to ASCII space.
  • Case is NOT mapped.
  • NFC normalization is applied.
  • There is no directionality rule, since it would reduce the allowed characters and passwords are rarely displayed.

Comparison is again octet-for-octet. Where a protocol hands the password to a hash function, the client must do the enforcement first, because the server never sees the plaintext.

Examples: correct horse battery staple and its capitalized form are different legal passwords; symbols such as the diamond suit (U+2666) are fine; an Ogham space mark (U+1680) becomes an ordinary space; a string containing a tab control character is not valid.
sections.eli5: A password can use almost any symbol, and different kinds of space all become a normal space. Capital letters still count, so "Cat" and "cat" are different passwords.

sections.title: Migrating from SASLprep
sections.content:
The rules differ slightly from RFC 4013 (SASLprep), so deployments may need to scrub data. The RFC points out three differences.

  • Normalization: SASLprep used NFKC, while these profiles use NFC. NFKC also mapped fullwidth and halfwidth characters, and turned code points like LATIN SMALL LIGATURE FI (U+FB01) into their compatibility equivalents. The username classes now forbid such code points. Operators may want to search for them and map them where there is no conflict; conflicting names (such as HENRYIV written with ROMAN NUMERAL FOUR) must be handled case by case, for example by disabling one account.
  • Mapped to nothing: SASLprep dropped "commonly mapped to nothing" characters. PRECIS now disallows most of them, so operators may remove them (for example SOFT HYPHEN, U+00AD) from stored usernames.
  • Case: SASLprep allowed uppercase, so UsernameCasePreserved matches it, while UsernameCaseMapped folds case.

For passwords, migration may need no data scrubbing if passwords are not stored in the clear, but some passwords that matched under SASLprep may stop working if they contain code points with compatibility equivalents.
sections.eli5: When a school changes its name rules, it has to check the old class lists for names that no longer fit. This part explains which old names might need a fix.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Security
sections.content:
IANA added three entries to the PRECIS Profiles registry: UsernameCaseMapped and UsernameCasePreserved (base class IdentifierClass) and OpaqueString (base class FreeformClass). Each is listed as replacing the SASLprep profile of stringprep, and IANA marked the SASLprep profile in the stringprep registry as "Not Current".

The security notes are short. Allowing a wide range of characters in passwords can raise entropy, but users must also be able to type those characters on various devices. Comparing identifiers can produce false negatives or false positives, both with security impact (discussed in RFC 6943). The security considerations of RFC 7564 and of Unicode Technical Standard #39 also apply.

The RFC also warns that being liberal in what you accept, which some PRECIS profiles encourage, can be problematic for usernames and passwords because it can lead to false positives.
sections.eli5: The main danger is two different things being mistaken for each other. Strange characters make better passwords, but only if you can actually type them on every device.
